item.title: Former Secret Service investigator sounds alarm over AI scams as Americans grow increasingly anxious
item.description: Former Secret Service cyberfraud investigator Jason Brown warns AI voice cloning scams could trick families into losing thousands of dollars this holiday season.
item.content:encoded:
A former Secret Service cyberfraud investigator warned that Americans are increasingly on edge following a wave of major technology disruptions, while artificial intelligence is making scams targeting families and consumers more sophisticated.

Jason Brown, a former U.S. Secret Service cyberfraud investigator and iCounter's director of customer advisory and counter fraud lead, told Fox News Digital on Thursday that Americans have reason to be increasingly cautious about technology.

"Everybody's on edge," Brown said.

"There's been a lot of stuff that has happened in the past week in particular that people are concerned about," he continued, citing recent technology outages involving Microsoft, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) and several financial institutions.

TIMELINE: AMERICA HITS A TECH WALL AS OUTAGES CRIPPLE EMAIL, GROUND FLIGHTS AND DISRUPT MAJOR BANKS

Brown acknowledged that some incidents involved infrastructure problems while others remained under investigation.

With the holiday season approaching, Brown warned that AI has made it easier for criminals to create convincing fraudulent messages, eliminating many of the warning signs consumers previously relied on.

"AI has just made the criminal a lot more efficient and a little bit more effective," Brown said.

Spelling mistakes, poor grammar and awkward phrasing — once common indicators of fraudulent messages — are becoming less reliable as criminals use AI to generate more convincing communications, he explained.

AI VOICE SCAM TRAPS MOM IN 5-HOUR KIDNAPPING NIGHTMARE

AI also allows criminals to impersonate familiar voices, potentially tricking victims into believing they are speaking with a family member in distress.

Brown described a scenario in which a scammer uses a short voice recording to impersonate someone's relative and demand thousands of dollars in gift cards.

"AI just makes them a lot more efficient and a lot less prone to errors," he said, warning that Americans must become more skeptical of suspicious messages.

"Unfortunately, we're at a point where everybody needs to have that level of distrust," he said.

As holiday shopping ramps up, Brown said scammers are likely to impersonate major delivery companies, including UPS, FedEx and the U.S. Postal Service.

FAKE E-ZPASS EMAIL THREATENS $100 FINE OVER UNPAID TOLL

He warned that fraudulent messages may claim packages cannot be delivered until additional postage is paid, with scammers demanding payment through cryptocurrency or gift cards.

"If it comes from crypto, especially if it comes from gift cards, that's a red flag for sure," Brown said.

Beyond the emotional toll, Brown warned that increasingly sophisticated scams can result in significant financial losses. He cited FBI reporting that he said identified more than 22,000 AI-related fraud cases in 2025, with losses exceeding $890 million.

Brown noted that businesses are also vulnerable to schemes in which criminals impersonate trusted vendors and redirect legitimate payments into fraudulent accounts.

AGING MEANS LEARNING HOW TO PREVENT COSTLY SCAMS TARGETING OLDER AMERICANS

The holiday season can create additional vulnerabilities as executives travel, employees take time off and temporary workers join company operations, he said.

Brown urged Americans to independently verify suspicious messages and take additional precautions when communicating with family members, including establishing a "safe word" to help confirm someone's identity during an unexpected call.

"Another thing that we always talk about with family members, set up a safe word ahead of time. Have that conversation now," he said, adding that even if a caller provides the correct word, people should still end the call and contact the person independently using a trusted number.

"The biggest safety valve for anybody in a scam when it comes over the internet via your cell phone over the computer is stop, think, and then independently verify," he added.

item.title: Texas inmate's execution takes over an hour as prison staff struggle to find suitable veins
item.description: Texas inmate Reinaldo Dennes repeatedly cried out in pain as prison staff struggled for over an hour to establish IV access for his lethal injection.
item.content:encoded:
A Texas inmate's execution lasted more than an hour Thursday as prison staff struggled to find suitable veins for a lethal injection, with the condemned man repeatedly complaining of severe pain before being pronounced dead.

Reinaldo Dennes, who was convicted of capital murder in the 1996 killing of Houston diamond dealer Janos Szucs, repeatedly cried out during the procedure at the state penitentiary in Huntsville, according to The Associated Press.

Dennes was pronounced dead at 7:08 p.m., one minute after the procedure was completed.

The procedure lasted 63 minutes from the time Dennes was strapped to the gurney until its completion, as prison staff struggled to find suitable veins for the intravenous needles used to administer pentobarbital.

CHRISTA PIKE'S EXECUTION DOCTOR SAYS MISPLACED IV SENT LETHAL DRUGS INTO HER ARMS INSTEAD OF VEINS

The execution comes amid renewed scrutiny of lethal injection procedures following a failed execution attempt in Tennessee in September involving death row inmate Christa Pike, who survived two doses of pentobarbital that her attorneys said did not properly enter her bloodstream, causing serious injuries.

Dennes repeatedly complained of pain after Thursday's procedure began, groaning and calling out to God, according to witnesses cited by The AP.

"The pain! Go! Go!" Dennes exclaimed.

"My right leg is killing me!" he later shouted, describing the sensation as a cramp.

"I don't think this is normal. Take me, father. Don't let me suffer like this. C'mon," he added.

CHRISTA PIKE'S ATTORNEYS SAY SHE'S IN CRITICAL CONDITION AFTER BOTCHED LETHAL INJECTIONS

Texas Department of Criminal Justice spokesperson Amanda Hernandez said all procedures were followed appropriately but acknowledged that staff made multiple unsuccessful attempts to establish IV access before placing needles in Dennes' left foot and the left side of his neck.

Hernandez said she did not know how many attempts were unsuccessful but maintained that the locations ultimately used complied with the state's execution procedures.

She also suggested that Dennes may have exaggerated his discomfort, noting that he complained of pain before the drugs began flowing and in areas where no IV had been placed.

According to The AP, when asked whether Dennes was faking his pain, she replied, "I think, yeah, there were allegations. ... There was nothing abnormal on our part."

INDIANA, FLORIDA AND ALABAMA CARRY OUT RARE US TRIPLE EXECUTION DAY

"This isn't the first time we had to insert IVs into other locations. It's also not the first time we've had an inmate make allegations of pain immediately," Hernandez said.

Dennes was the second person executed in the United States on Thursday, following Florida's execution of Thomas Mitchell Overton, 71, who was convicted of killing a pregnant woman and her husband during a home invasion.

Overton's execution marked Florida's 20th of the year, a state record, according to the AP.

Fox News Digital has reached out to the Texas Department of Criminal Justice for additional comment.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

item.title: Pro-life group says Trump admin didn't give key abortion drug commitments before Overton FDA nomination pulled
item.description: Susan B. Anthony Pro-Life America opposed Heidi Overton's FDA confirmation until the Trump administration committed to ending mail-order abortion drugs.
item.content:encoded:
A leading pro-life group said it opposed advancing Heidi Overton's nomination to lead the Food and Drug Administration without commitments from the Trump administration on abortion drug policy. The White House withdrew her nomination this week amid questions about her support in the Senate.

In an interview with Fox News Digital, Erik Baptist, senior vice president of legal strategy at Susan B. Anthony Pro-Life America, said his group asked the Senate to hold up Overton’s confirmation until it received "firm commitments" from the administration on two fronts regarding abortion drug policy.

Baptist said the group wants the next FDA nominee to commit to ending mail-order access to abortion drugs authorized under the Biden administration and changing how the agency studies the safety of those pills.

"Right now, we’re seeing more abortions in this country than before the Supreme Court’s decision overturning Roe v. Wade," Baptist said. "That’s precisely because of what the Biden FDA did to authorize mail-order abortion drugs. We’re seeing upwards of 15,000 abortion drugs and abortions occurring in pro-life states. Those states can’t meaningfully enforce their laws while this nationwide policy is in place."

WHITE HOUSE PULLS TRUMP'S FDA PICK HEIDI OVERTON ON EVE OF SENATE PANEL VOTE

"Under the Biden-era policy, anybody can obtain these drugs online and receive them through the mail," he continued. "When I say anybody, we’ve seen news story after news story every week about men and other predators obtaining these drugs to coerce or poison women into taking them against their will. Until that policy changes, no pregnant woman is safe from these drugs. My question to this administration is: How many more women have to be poisoned or coerced with abortion drugs before you take action on this drug?"

Under the Biden administration, the FDA eliminated the in-person dispensing requirement for mifepristone, allowing it to be prescribed without an in-person visit by certified prescribers and dispensed by certified pharmacies through the mail.

On the group's second point of concern, Baptist said the FDA needs to conduct a new study to show the safety — or lack thereof — of mifepristone.

"The problem is that the study is significantly flawed," he said. "It’s almost designed to fail and not lead to future changes to the drug regimen. We have asked for more robust data because significant information is currently lacking, including transparency into the agency’s methodology and an invitation for outside experts who have studied this drug over the last few decades."

"This is something that should be bipartisan. Everybody should support better data, more transparency and outside experts who can inform an agency that has never conducted such a study before," he added.

Several pro-life groups and Republican lawmakers have urged the Trump administration to complete the FDA’s safety review of mifepristone and consider reinstating safeguards, while some have called for removing the drug from the market.

The FDA said the review is ongoing, with study results expected in December 2026 and a final report expected by March 2027.

The White House pulled Overton’s nomination to lead the FDA earlier this week, one day before a Senate committee vote. President Donald Trump picked Overton, a physician and White House advisor, in August to succeed Marty Makary, who resigned from the position in May.

Kyle Diamantas has led the agency in an acting capacity since Makary’s departure.

WOMAN WHO SAYS ABORTION PILLS NEARLY KILLED HER URGES RFK JR TO ACT AS GROUP DEMANDS MAIL-ORDER CRACKDOWN

Overton also previously served as vice chair and chief policy officer at the America First Policy Institute, a conservative think tank, where she criticized expanded access to abortion pills in a 2023 policy brief.

The White House said Overton lacked the votes on Capitol Hill and pulled her nomination, although Sen. Bill Cassidy, chair of the Senate health committee, contended that he believed she could have been confirmed.

"The White House abandoned a viable confirmation path for Dr. Overton. The WH said that this was because she did not have the votes to pass. This was odd as I was having productive conversations with members," Cassidy, R-La., wrote on X. "I believe she would have had the votes to pass out of committee and pass the full Senate."

Baptist said he did not know whether the White House was concerned about pro-life votes or other constituencies but thinks Cassidy "was making progress with the administration to secure the commitments we were seeking and asking the Senate to hold the administration accountable for."

Cassidy had criticized Overton for supporting Trump’s decision to recommend changes to the childhood vaccine schedule, but the senator said he had been convinced she was right for the job after she committed to "follow the science." She had appeared alongside Trump in the Oval Office as the president signed an executive order calling for changes to childhood vaccine recommendations, including a recommendation to administer measles, mumps and rubella vaccines separately once individual shots become available domestically.

Cassidy said at a September hearing that there was no scientific evidence for Trump’s suggestion that the combined shot could be "quite lethal" and warned the remark could discourage vaccination.

"Yes, senator, the MMR vaccine is safe and effective," Overton told Cassidy.

Pressed on what she would do if Trump asked her to disregard the FDA’s safety standards, Overton said she would give the president her best advice and follow the legal requirements for reviewing individual products.

Sen. Maggie Hassan, D-N.H., asked Overton directly whether Trump was wrong. Overton reiterated that the vaccine was safe and effective and called it the best tool available during the measles outbreak. Sen. Ed Markey, D-Mass., questioned why she had not corrected Trump in the Oval Office.

"Why should we expect you to stand up to the president as FDA commissioner?" Markey asked.

Baptist said he wants the next FDA commissioner to be somebody who "understands science" and has experience managing an agency.

"The FDA is a very large bureaucracy with multiple constituencies, so understanding how science is conducted and how drugs are approved will be essential to any successful candidate or nominee for the position," he said.

But, Baptist said, the administration does not have to wait for an FDA nominee to take the position before it can take the action on abortion pill policy that his group desires.

"The good news is that it doesn’t have to be the nominee who makes these commitments. The administration can do it because it has admitted that it can take these actions immediately using its own authority," he argued. "That power is within the administration’s possession. It’s a matter of political will, not legal ability."

"With regard to fixing the study, I think they can make those changes now," Baptist continued. "They don’t need to wait for a confirmation, especially when they’re saying they’re going to finish the study in December of this year. We might not have an FDA commissioner at that point, or even a nominee. So they need to fix it immediately and course-correct the study before it’s fatally flawed and completed next year."

Fox News' Stepheny Price contributed to this report.

item.title: Texans finally get first win at home in 2026 season, dismantling lowly Colts to keep playoff dreams alive
item.description: C.J. Stroud's 42-yard strike to Nico Collins and a suffocating Texans defense crushed Daniel Jones as Houston snapped its 0-4 home skid at NRG Stadium.
item.content:encoded:
Houston Texans fans can finally cheer for their team winning a home game at Reliant Stadium this season — even if it was a layup.

The Texans were 12.5-point favorites entering "Thursday Night Football" against the Indianapolis Colts, their AFC South foe who they lost to earlier this season, and they showed why with a thrashing to improve to 4-6 on the year with a 26-3 win.

There was hope the Colts would come out with some fight against a division opponent and play competitively despite the fire sale before the NFL trade deadline, during which four key starters were sent to contenders.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

Indianapolis did pick up a win at home against the Miami Dolphins last week, but against an actual competitive squad like the Texans, they were no match.

And if this game was any indication of how the Colts will play the remainder of the season amid their clear rebuild, well, we’re going to feel for players like running back Jonathan Taylor through it.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Texans fans don’t care what the situation is for the Colts, though, as they were loud and proud on Thursday night with a 17-3 halftime lead thanks to clean quarterback play by C.J. Stroud, and some highlight-reel grabs by his receivers.

The first touchdown of the game was a 42-yard strike to top dog Nico Collins, who battled a defender and made the grab in the end zone for a 7-3 lead after the extra point.

Then, Kayshon Boutte climbed the ladder on his own Colts defender, hauling in a 24-yard pass from Stroud for the second-quarter score.

Houston’s drives were methodical, while its strong defense overpowered Daniel Jones to the point where the game was lost despite getting the first points on the board with a Spencer Shrader field goal.

Colts fans were already calling for head coach Shane Steichen to bench Jones after a dismal performance despite the win over the Dolphins last week. They got their wish in the fourth quarter.

With rookie tight end Marlin Klein scoring the first touchdown of his career in the third quarter, and Will Anderson Jr. sacking Jones in the end zone for a safety, the score was out of reach enough that Steichen called for Anthony Richardson Jr., the fourth overall pick in the 2023 NFL Draft who didn’t pan out in his time starting for Indy, to take some reps.

Also noteworthy: David Montgomery, in his first game back with the Texans since suffering his groin injury in Week 5, looked strong with 26 carries for 107 yards, while making three receptions for 17 yards as well.

It wasn’t the least bit competitive, but Texans fans are sure happy they got a win at home when they were supposed to considering they were 0-4 prior, and had some rough losses in Houston.

More importantly, if the Texans have any hope at making a run to the playoffs, it was a necessary victory to keep that dream alive.

item.title: WNBA star Caitlin Clark reveals unwavering loyalty to Notre Dame football after going incognito
item.description: Caitlin Clark told the "New Heights" podcast that Notre Dame recruited her, and she secretly attended their game against Miami earlier this month.
item.content:encoded:
We all know that Caitlin Clark plays for the Indiana Fever, a WNBA team based in the same state as Notre Dame in South Bend.

After playing her college basketball at Iowa, Clark now plays much closer to her favorite college football team, the Notre Dame Fighting Irish. During an appearance this week on Jason Kelce and Travis Kelce's "New Heights" podcast, Clark spoke out about her Notre Dame loyalty, which dates back to her childhood.

Clark is such a staunch Fighting Irish supporter, that she admitted she wore a disguise to go see Notre Dame play Miami earlier this month. Notre Dame defeated Miami, then the No. 1 team in the nation, 31-24 in a game that was marked by late-game controversy.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

"I had on like a hat and sunglasses, and I was actually in the second to last row of like the normal bowl, like normal seats. Yeah, nobody knew, I mean some people knew," Clark said.

"People around me knew, but like the thing that's like the fun part about football in the fall is like just actually like being in the environment and like the experience of college football is so fun ... Tailgated a little bit. Jason Sudeikis was the guest picker that week. He was hanging out with us. He's a big, big Chiefs fan himself, so he's a great guy."

CAITLIN CLARK TELLS KYLIE KELCE SHE WANTS 'TO BE LOYAL TO THE RED' AFTER COLTS' BLUE JERSEY CONTROVERSY

The Fighting Irish women's basketball team also recruited Clark as she was preparing to take the leap from high school to the college level.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

"I try to make it to, like, one Notre Dame game a year. I grew up a Notre Dame fan. I wanted to go to Notre Dame," she noted. "They recruited me. It was between Notre Dame and Iowa, and then I picked Iowa. But Notre Dame is just so cool – the history of everything. And then a night game, you're playing the number one team in the country."

Clark also made a surprise appearance at Penn’s men’s basketball game against Illinois in Champaign on Nov. 5. Fran McCaffery, the father of Clark’s boyfriend, Connor McCaffery, is in his second season as Penn's head coach.

Many of the Illinois players did not realize Clark was in attendance until after the game, prompting a jaw-dropping reaction from Quentin Coleman. "Wait, Caitlin was in the building?" Coleman said. "Yoooo! I gotta tell my sister, bro."

NOTRE DAME FOOTBALL HOLDS MICHIGAN STATE TO 167 TOTAL YARDS IN 27-10 HOME VICTORY

Clark also showed off her football fandom earlier this year as a celebrity guest picker on ESPN’s "College GameDay." She also helped energize the Iowa fans that were on hand before the Hawkeyes' matchup with Ohio State.

Clark earned her third consecutive WNBA All-Star selection this year. Clark and the Fever were eliminated in the first round of the playoffs after losing to the Las Vegas Aces.

item.title: Senate Republicans break through Washington gridlock with massive American energy, data center overhaul
item.description: Senate Republicans advanced a sweeping permitting bill to speed environmental review, expand the electric grid and limit legal challenges on projects.
item.content:encoded:
Senate Republicans scored a major win after advancing a massive bill that would overhaul America’s permitting system in a bid to turbocharge infrastructure and energy development in the country.

The Senate advanced the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 (BAAJA) on a major bipartisan vote Thursday night. The legislation went through fits and starts over the last few months, until a bipartisan coalition, with buy-in from the White House, formed to tinker with the final product.

At the 30,000-foot level, the sweeping package would accelerate environmental review of projects, limit legal challenges, protect approved projects, expand the electric grid and streamline energy development in all fields — like oil, gas and renewables.

AMERICA’S BROKEN PERMITTING SYSTEM IS QUIETLY RAISING YOUR COST OF LIVING

"This is a major step toward making it faster and more efficient and easier to build infrastructure projects, certainly without giving up any of the strong protections for our environment," Chair of the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee Shelley Moore Capito, R-W.Va., said when the bill was introduced in September.

The bill also tackles an issue that was front and center for voters across the country: data centers.

Sen. Martin Heinrich, D-N.M., the Democratic lead on the legislation, pushed for stronger language in the bill that would shield ratepayers from higher costs that stem from data center development and their usage of electricity.

WHO PAYS FOR US POWER BOOM? BLUE, RED STATES OFFER STARKLY DIFFERENT WAYS TO LOWER UTILITY BILLS AMID AI SURGE

That comes after Republicans tried to ram through similar safeguards before the election with a bill from Sen. Jon Husted, R-Ohio, that Democrats argued lacked real enforcement teeth.

"This process will mean that we develop responsibly. It will mean more jobs. It will mean cheaper energy," Heinrich said. "It will mean that we actually require big load centers, whether that's a factory or a data center, to not pass those costs on to the American consumer by statute, not a suggestion, an actual law."

The provision covers data centers with a demand of at least 20 megawatts of power, and would require them to cover the cost of additional power for them to run, financial guarantees covering costs to build or upgrade facilities, to pay the tab if they leave an area for unpaid infrastructure costs, allow states to charge higher rates to reduce other customers’ bills and tack on power supply conditions.

DEMS KILL REPUBLICAN'S CHANCES OF LOWERING AMERICANS' ELECTRICITY BILLS IN KEY ELECTION FLASHPOINT

Meanwhile, whether the legislation makes it through the House is an open question.

Sen. Alan Armstrong, R-Okla., who was appointed to the position earlier this year to replace Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin and has made permitting reform his primary policy issue, told Fox News Digital that there were "a lot of good supporters on both sides of the aisle in the House." But he worried about attendance issues in the lower chamber.

"A lot of the language that's in here came right out of a lot of the House’s work," Armstrong said. "So, I think there'll be some support. I just hope we have people, you know, show up in the numbers that we need to vote for it."

item.title: Quinnipiac University's lockdown lifted after reports of possible gunman
item.description: Quinnipiac University was placed on lockdown Thursday evening in response to a possible gunman on campus, according to university officials.
item.content:encoded:
The lockdown at Quinnipiac University was lifted for the Mount Carmel Campus at around 2:30 a.m. Friday following reports of a possible gunman on campus, according to university officials.

"The lockdown has been lifted at the Mount Carmel Campus. Emergency response officials have completed a thorough sweep of all campus buildings and determined it is safe to resume normal activities," the university said on social media.

The university lifted its York Hill and North Haven campuses shortly after 10:30 p.m. Thursday.

Officials said classes for Friday were canceled and that counselors will be available to students.

TEEN ACCUSED OF FATALLY SHOOTING IDENTICAL TWIN BROTHER AFTER FIGHT ABOUT TOUCHING HIS BELONGINGS

"University classes will be canceled Friday, Nov. 20. Counselors will be available to students in person and via Zoom on the Mount Carmel and North Haven campuses starting at 9 a.m.," the university said shortly after 11 p.m.

While the Mount Carmel campus was still on lockdown, families and friends of students who were waiting outside of campus were told they could come to the Rocky Top Student Center on the York Hill Campus to wait for updates.

An earlier alert instructed people on campus to shelter in place as police responded to reports of a possible gunman.

"Please stay inside," the university said on social media. "There are reports of a possible gunman on campus."

"There is a heavy police presence on campus to deal with this matter," the post said.

The alert was also sent via text message to the campus community.

IVY LEAGUE STUDENT SLASHED IN NECK, SUSPECT ACCUSED WAS ARRESTED JUST WEEKS BEFORE

A university spokesperson told Fox News Digital that the reported threat prompted a response from local police, but officers had not yet found the suspected gunman.

The latest alert did not say whether a gunman was located.

item.title: Army delays controlled detonation of unstable bomb-making chemical in Iowa
item.description: The Army postponed the controlled detonation of 68 drums of lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, citing a temperature drop.
item.content:encoded:
The U. S. Army postponed Friday's planned controlled detonation of five tons of unstable bomb-making chemicals at an Iowa munitions plant until Monday, Nov. 23, amid an incoming temperature drop, environmental lawsuits and a call to delay the blast from Iowa Gov. Kim Reynolds.

Acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle directed Army Materiel Command to push back the operation at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, placing the detonation at the latest possible window before the weather shifts.

"Public safety is the Army’s top priority, and I have directed Army Materiel Command to postpone tomorrow’s controlled detonation at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa until Monday, November 23," Telle said in a statement on X.

IOWA RESIDENTS NEAR AMMUNITION PLANT TOLD TO VACATE BEFORE ARMY DETONATES 5 TONS OF BOMB-MAKING CHEMICALS

"This will delay the detonation until the latest possible moment prior to a forecasted temperature drop, which would risk further destabilization of the material," the statement added.

The pause came after Reynolds urged the Army to delay the operation amid growing public safety concerns in the region, while environmental groups filed lawsuits seeking to halt the planned detonation.

The decision delays a temporary evacuation for the roughly 400 residents of Middletown, who had been advised to leave their homes Friday morning due to "the potential for localized window damage" and a dust plume containing lead particles.

Crews are preparing to detonate 68 drums of degraded lead azide, a chemical used to set off munitions that had been stored in bunkers at the plant for more than 20 years. Army officials discovered in March that water had evaporated from the barrels' stabilizing bath, allowing the material to recrystallize and become too unstable to handle or relocate safely.

"The recrystallization of lead azide has created a risk of spontaneous explosion due to the material’s sensitivity to friction and shock, creating a highly unstable and dangerous situation," the Environmental Protection Agency said earlier this month when approving an emergency permit for the blast.

CALIFORNIA OFFICIALS WARN MASSIVE CHEMICAL TANK WILL LIKELY SPILL THOUSANDS OF GALLONS OR 'BLOW UP'

An Army smoke model released Tuesday projected the plume could reach 25 miles north to Wapello, Iowa, and spread across parts of eastern Iowa and northwest Illinois, potentially settling on farmland and playgrounds. The model also noted that "Children under six are especially vulnerable to lead exposure."

The Army said it will continue coordinating with the EPA and state and local officials to share updated safety and evacuation guidance ahead of Monday's rescheduled detonation.

Fox News Digital's Greg Norman-Diamond contributed to this report.

item.title: Feds release brazen heist video, charge 14 in alleged $22.5M California freight train theft ring
item.description: Fourteen suspects face federal charges in an alleged $22.5 million cargo theft scheme targeting 36 freight trains in Southern California.
item.content:encoded:
At least 14 suspects have been federally charged with orchestrating a $22.5 million cargo theft scheme that targeted at least 36 freight trains in Southern California, the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Central District of California announced Thursday.

The crew's leader was identified as Nathan Daniel Angel, 21, of East Los Angeles, who allegedly ran the operation alongside his father and two uncles.

Officials also released video of the brazen heist that appeared to have been filmed by some of the crew members. In the clip, members are seen sawing through cargo doors, grabbing boxes and flashing peace signs as they ransacked the trains.

"The scale of the theft is staggering," First Assistant United States Attorney Bill Essayli said. "We will prosecute the people who raid these trains and those who knowingly turn stolen cargo into cash."

CARGO THEFT HITS EVERYTHING FROM LEGO TO TEQUILA. WE NEED THE SENATE TO HELP STOP IT

HUNDREDS OF THOUSANDS OF DOLLARS IN STOLEN GOODS RECOVERED AT A USED CAR LOT AFTER ADULT TOY COMPANY PURCHASE

From February 2024 to August 2026, Nathan Angel allegedly led a group of co-conspirators in targeting freight trains carrying high-value goods for resale on the black market.

The trains reportedly carried Nike sneakers, Milwaukee tools, electronics and other products that entered the U.S. through the Ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach from international destinations.

According to prosecutors, Nathan Angel and his co-conspirators allegedly planned their thefts in advance by selecting specific locations along railroad tracks where they could force trains to stop.

Once the trains reached these preselected locations, members of the group cut the air hoses to trigger an emergency stop, officials alleged.

As the trains came to a halt, other crew members allegedly used trucks or vans to drive to the designated locations and board the trains, while additional members acted as lookouts.

The alleged thieves then transported the goods to stash houses, including properties belonging to some of the suspects.

The crew then coordinated their thefts through Instagram while discussing resale prices for the stolen products, prosecutors alleged.

NEARLY $1M IN GRADED TRADING CARDS STOLEN FROM FEDEX TRUCK OUTSIDE PSA FACILITY IN SANTA ANA

Officials said one buyer was a representative of a Los Angeles-based business known as a sneaker and streetwear resale brand. The business was not an authorized Nike reseller, officials said.

That business alone reportedly generated more than $1 million for the crew by purchasing thousands of pairs of stolen Nike sneakers between May 2025 and October 2025.

The crew leader's family members named in the case include his father, Daniel Angel, 38, of East Los Angeles, and his uncles, Rodolfo Angel, 23, and Jose Luis Angel, 23, both of East Los Angeles.

The other defendants include Donta Hedgeman, 27, Fernando Alexis Alvarado Villegas, 27, Daniel Garcia, 36, Carlos Robert Estrada, 28, Angel Sanchez, 24, Ruben Mario Banuelos, 26, Fredy Marquina, 25, Carlos Luis Fernando Martinez, 23, Jorge Angel Aguilar Espinoza, 36, and Ricardo Mares, 32.

"Train robberies cause enormous economic damage because of the valuable cargo involved. These defendants face long federal prison sentences if convicted. All are presumed innocent until proven guilty," Essayli said.

The arrests followed a 14-month investigation that involved the Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), the Los Angeles Police Department Commercial Crimes Bureau, the Union Pacific Railroad Police Department, the California Highway Patrol Cargo Theft Interdiction Program and the IRS Criminal Investigation.

If convicted, the defendants face maximum federal prison sentences of five years for conspiracy and 10 years per theft count. Additionally, each count of violence against railroad cars carries a maximum penalty of life in prison.

item.title: Deion Sanders receives 'about five' death threats every day as Colorado football coach
item.description: Deion Sanders gets about five death threats a day, per The Athletic, which obtained 15 closed harassment cases since he took over Colorado football.
item.content:encoded:
Just a few years ago, Colorado’s football program had largely been forgotten. Then Pro Football Hall of Famer Deion Sanders arrived in Boulder, bringing his larger-than-life personality and celebrity to the program.

Colorado’s on-field results under Sanders have been uneven, but his tenure has also been marked by significant off-field challenges. Sanders has continued coaching while managing serious health issues. More recently, police records obtained by The Athletic detailed how his personal safety has been at risk at times.

According to a September report, Sanders regularly received death threats. At one point, he said he was receiving "about five" threats per day. Public records from Boulder shed light on how authorities handled many of those situations.

In May 2023, a pair of university police officers waited for Sanders outside his office. Once the two-time Super Bowl winner met the officers, they told Sanders about a series of threatening voicemails on a Colorado football ticket office phone line that mentioned him.

item.content:encoded:

item.title: LSU poked the SEC bear, then folded: RJ Luis benched after conference leaders discussed expulsion or boycott
item.description: Sources tell OutKick SEC schools weighed boycotting games against LSU and expelling the Tigers before the school benched RJ Luis amid the legal fight.
item.content:encoded:
One day after Will Wade sent RJ Luis onto the court, LSU has backed down from its latest fight with the SEC.

LSU President Wade Rousse announced late Thursday afternoon that the Tigers would no longer play Luis, abruptly reversing course after the former professional basketball player scored 11 points in Wednesday night’s win over Louisiana-Monroe.

"In my role as president of the LSU System, after further review, I have instructed LSU men's basketball coach Will Wade not to play RJ Luis," Rousse said.

LANE KIFFIN’S ROSTER FIGHT SET THE STAGE, WILL WADE JUST THREW A GRENADE IN LSU-SEC WAR WITH RJ LUIS

That’s quite the turnaround from the message Wade delivered after Wednesday’s game.

"He was eligible, and he played," Wade said.

For a school locked in a federal lawsuit with the SEC over the roster battle involving Lane Kiffin’s football program in September, playing Luis was another escalation.

Less than 24 hours later, LSU put down its sword related to the basketball player.

Not even 24 hours after RJ Luis scored 11 points in the LSU win, the Tigers waived the white flag regarding this fight that involved their basketball team.

Why the sudden change of heart?

SEC presidents were already scheduled to hold a call Thursday afternoon to discuss several topics. But after Luis played Wednesday night, the conversation was set to take on a different tone.

ATTORNEY COMPARES SEC COMMISSIONER GREG SANKEY TO ‘KIM JONG’ IN LSU-RJ LUIS ELIGIBILITY LAWSUIT

Multiple sources told OutKick that options including SEC schools boycotting games against LSU and renewed discussions about potentially expelling the Tigers from the conference were back on the table.

"That was the final straw for SEC leaders, they were ready to penalize them (LSU) in some form or fashion," one source familiar with the discussions told OutKick. "You can only poke the bear so many times before they decide to pounce, and they (SEC Presidents and Chancellors) had seen enough nonsense from LSU.

"Who knows if they would have actually boycotted games, or even tried. But, lawyers from schools within the conference were going through their options. This whole thing is just annoying. Like, get your sh-t together, and I mean everyone involved."

SEC FILES BOMBSHELL LAWSUIT AGAINST LSU, LANE KIFFIN WHILE PRO PLAYERS FIGHT FOR COLLEGE ELIGIBILITY IN COURT

Sources also told OutKick that SEC Commissioner Greg Sankey spoke with Rousse on Thursday afternoon before the scheduled presidents’ meeting, delivering a blunt and honest assessment of the thinking of conference leaders of what could happen if LSU continued playing Luis.

The message apparently landed.

Less than two hours after the conversation with Sankey and consultations with its own general counsel, LSU announced that Luis would no longer play. Rousse did not participate in the full call with the other SEC presidents.

LSU’s decision does not necessarily mean Luis is finished fighting.

The former professional football players involved in the separate LSU eligibility case are still considering a civil lawsuit against the SEC over what they contend was interference with their court-ordered ability to play.

Could Luis pursue some type of damages of his own? A statement from one of his attorneys suggests this dispute could be far from over.

"The SEC's decision to threaten a member with expulsion if it plays an eligible student-athlete is reprehensible and seriously harms a young person who was caught in the middle of a power struggle having nothing to do with him," one of RJ Luis's attorneys, Elliot Abrams, said in a statement.

COLLEGE ATHLETICS' LATEST MESS: COURT ORDERS SAY PRO ATHLETES CAN PLAY, BUT SEC AND BIG TEN READY TO FIGHT

The latest showdown began last Friday, when a Baton Rouge judge granted Luis a preliminary injunction. The scope of that order — and whether its protections extended to LSU playing him — became a central point of contention.

In a statement Monday, the SEC said it would abide by the order and would not punish LSU for rostering Luis.

Playing him was another matter.

On Tuesday, the conference made clear that it disagreed with LSU’s interpretation of the court order.

"LSU’s decision today to rely on its own interpretation of the Court’s order to justify its actions is inconsistent with the expectations and responsibilities of [SEC membership]. This is a deeply concerning and disappointing development."

The SEC wants to enforce its membership rules. LSU relied on its interpretation of a Baton Rouge judge’s order to put a former professional player on the court.

On Wednesday night, the Tigers tested how far they could push that argument.

By Thursday afternoon, they had their answer.

This basketball dispute is another chapter in a fight that had already spilled into federal court.

Three months ago, the SEC filed a federal lawsuit against LSU as Sankey testified in a Baton Rouge courtroom in the case brought by Dae’Quan Wright and Zxavian Harris, who were seeking to play football for Kiffin’s Tigers.

The federal case has since produced its own stream of legal jabs.

On Wednesday, the SEC asked a judge to strike language from LSU’s motion to dismiss in which the school’s attorneys accused the conference of making "hallucinated" claims against a defendant.

A judge ordered LSU’s lawyers to issue a public apology through a press release. Louisiana Attorney General Liz Murrill pushed back in a filing, telling the court that would not happen.

LSU LEAVES FORMER PRO-ATHLETES OFF FINAL ROSTER, ONE NIGHT BEFORE SEC TAKES LANE KIFFIN AND TIGERS TO COURT

That same day, attorney Tony Clayton, representing Luis, filed a motion seeking to hold the SEC in contempt over the conference’s Tuesday statement.

So, yes, there were already plenty of reasons for tension between LSU and its conference before Wade sent Luis into Wednesday’s game.

Playing him amounted to throwing another grenade into an ongoing legal battle.

Now, LSU has retreated on the basketball front, leaving Luis sidelined while the broader fight continues.

Will that open the door for peace talks between LSU and the SEC?

Given the lawsuits, threats and courtroom clashes hanging over this relationship, I wouldn’t count on a ceasefire just yet.

Davies, who was Senate-confirmed, will join Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton, White House technology advisor Michael Kratsios and Secretary of State Marco Rubio on the administration's national security and cyber leadership team.

It has been my pleasure to work closely with Kirsten on national security matters, and I look forward to now working with her to navigate an increasingly dynamic and fast-moving cyber landscape."

Under President Trump’s leadership we will have a more secure, resilient; and supercharged technological future," Davies wrote. "I am honored to continue to serve."

The leadership shakeup follows a nearly weeklong stretch of technical disruptions that hit air travel, major banks, Microsoft services, Apple, Marriott, the National Weather Service and internal systems at the National Security Agency.

item.title: EXCLUSIVE: Retired police sergeant issues warning over Mamdani's NYPD shake-up ahead of Thanksgiving parade
item.description: New York City's Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade could face security gaps after the NYPD's Strategic Response Group disbandment, a retired sergeant warns.
item.content:encoded:
EXCLUSIVE: A retired police sergeant with nearly three decades of law enforcement experience warned that she would not bring her own family to New York City amid Mayor Zohran Mamdani's plans to dismantle a specialized NYPD unit responsible for counterterrorism support and crowd control.

"I wouldn't take my family there right now," retired Sgt. Betsy Brantner Smith, a spokesperson for the National Police Association, told Fox News Digital in an exclusive interview.

Smith's warning follows Mamdani's announcement that the NYPD's Strategic Response Group (SRG), a roughly 500-officer specialized unit involved in counterterrorism, major event security and protest response, will be disbanded as part of a broader overhaul of how the nation's largest police department handles demonstrations.

MAMDANI GUTS ELITE NYPD TACTICAL UNIT, BACKS 'CIVILIAN-LED APPROACH' TO RESPONDING TO PROTESTS

The democratic socialist mayor has defended the decision as fulfilling a campaign promise to separate counterterrorism operations from the policing of constitutionally protected protests. 

Critics, however, argue that dismantling the established unit could undermine the coordination and specialized training needed to respond to emergencies.

Smith, who spent 29 years in Chicago-area law enforcement and has experience supervising crowd control operations, said the consequences could extend beyond protests.

"One of the beauties of this strategic response group is that these are a group of officers who are used to working together," Smith said. "They train together. They have specialized knowledge of how to deal quickly and safely with these types of situations, including an active shooter."

MAMDANI PREPARES TO FULFILL PROMISE TO AXE NYPD UNIT RESPONSIBLE FOR CONTROLLING PROTEST VIOLENCE

Her concerns come as New York City prepares for the 100th Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade Nov. 26, an event expected to draw enormous crowds of visitors to Manhattan.

Smith warned that breaking up the specialized unit could create vulnerabilities if its responsibilities were redistributed without preserving existing operational relationships.

"First and foremost, I'm concerned that any intelligence may be lost or may be ignored for a large scale event like this," she said.

NYPD Assistant Commissioner Brad Weeks told Fox News Digital the restructuring will not affect security arrangements for this year's Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade, explaining that the new First Amendment Support Team and Patrol Support Division will not begin operating until February 2027.

FLORIDA EYES POACHING NYPD OFFICERS AFTER MAMDANI DISMANTLES ELITE UNIT

The department also said counterterrorism personnel currently assigned to the Strategic Response Group will be transferred to the NYPD's Counterterrorism Bureau, consolidating those capabilities within the specialized bureau.

In response to Fox News Digital's request for comment, Mamdani's office directed the outlet to remarks the mayor delivered during a news conference earlier this week.

"I've long said that counterterrorism and protest response are fundamentally different responsibilities and that New Yorkers exercising their constitutional right to protest should not be met with the same police response as a terrorism threat," Mamdani said.

The overhaul also imposes new restrictions on police tactics during protests, including prohibitions on long guns and tear gas, according to the mayor's office. 

Pepper spray will no longer be permitted as a general crowd management tool, while officers assigned to the new Patrol Support Division will receive specialized training and retain arrest powers when necessary.

MAMDANI UNVEILS SWEEPING NYPD USE-OF-FORCE REVIEW, BUT STOPS SHORT OF FULFILLING KEY CAMPAIGN PROMISES

Mamdani said the initial changes would take effect in approximately 90 days, with a First Amendment Support Team (FAST) operating within the NYPD's Community Affairs Bureau during the transition.

A separate civilian-led Community Dialogue and De-escalation Division, housed within the Office of Community Safety, is scheduled to launch in 2028. 

The mayor said the division would focus on engaging with protest organizers, mediation and preventing tensions from escalating.

Mamdani rejected suggestions that civilians would be expected to confront violent demonstrators without police support.

"Now, police will always be present in the case of any kind of violence," he said. "So this idea that New Yorkers' safety will be compromised is not true."

FAR-LEFT GROUPS CHEER MAMDANI FOR DISBANDING ELITE NYPD PROTEST TEAM

Smith, however, questioned whether the new approach could preserve the capabilities of officers accustomed to responding together during major incidents.

"It is a political decision on his part. And it's an incredibly dangerous one," she said.

NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch defended the restructuring, saying the department would maintain the resources necessary to respond to serious threats.

"I would never support changes that diminish the NYPD's ability to protect New Yorkers or that put our officers in a position where they lack the resources necessary to confront a serious threat," Tisch said in the city's announcement.

Mamdani's announcement also drew praise from far-left activist organizations that have long criticized the NYPD's handling of demonstrations.

NYC MAYOR ZOHRAN MAMDANI SAYS HE WON'T FIRE NYPD COMMISSIONER JESSICA TISCH DESPITE SOCIALIST PRESSURE

As Fox News Digital reported Wednesday, the Party for Socialism and Liberation celebrated the decision, declaring in a social media post that "the mass movement has won the disbanding of NYPD’s Strategic Response Group — but the fight continues."

Nerdeen Kiswani, founder of the anti-Israel activist organization Within Our Lifetime, also welcomed the announcement, describing it as "overdue and welcome news."

Self-described Marxist streamer Hasan Piker also praised the move, writing that he was "glad the mayor is moving on this promise to disband."

Fox News Digital's earlier reporting noted that it remained unclear whether those organizations or influencers had influenced the self-described democratic socialist mayor's decision.

MAMDANI'S LUXURY SECOND HOME TAX HITSD $500M MILESTONE DESPITE THOUSANDS OF EXEMPTIONS

The National Police Association has launched a Change.org petition urging Mamdani to reverse the decision to disband the Strategic Response Group, arguing that its specialized capabilities are essential to public safety.

According to the petition's organizers, nearly 2,000 people signed it within its first two days.

Smith urged the mayor to preserve the NYPD's ability to deploy officers with established training and experience.

"We urge the mayor of New York City to continue to allow the NYPD to do everything in its power to keep the city safe," she said.

Fox News Digital's Asra Nomani and Preston Mizell contributed to this reporting.

item.title: Democrat lawmaker hit with federal indictment over alleged $240K COVID fraud scheme
item.description: Alabama Rep. Patrick Sellers allegedly obtained more than $240,000 through fraudulent applications and used the money for personal expenses.
item.content:encoded:
An Alabama state representative has been indicted for allegedly orchestrating an extensive fraud scheme to obtain private and taxpayer-backed loans and grants to fund his personal expenses, the Justice Department announced Thursday.

Officials identified the lawmaker as Patrick Lorn Sellers, 53, who has represented a district near Birmingham since November 2022 and was recently re-elected to a second term. 

Sellers was also a church pastor and former chief of staff to the president of the Alabama State Missionary Baptist Convention (ASMBC).

Between July 2020 and May 2021, Sellers allegedly siphoned more than $240,000 in grants and loans intended to provide relief during the COVID-19 pandemic, according to the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Northern District of Alabama.

MINNESOTA FRAUD MASTERMIND GETS NEARLY 42 YEARS IN PRISON IN MASSIVE $250M 'FEEDING OUR FUTURE' SCHEME

The alleged scheme specifically targeted the federal and state governments and a private nonprofit.

Those benefits were used to cover personal expenses, including credit card bills, mortgage payments, auto loan payments, water bills and even his daughters' college tuition, officials said.

In one notable instance, Sellers allegedly took control of an affiliate nonprofit belonging to ASMBC and applied for pandemic relief funds without notifying the convention’s president or board.

After Sellers obtained the money, the charity's actual leaders were denied funding when they legitimately attempted to apply for assistance, officials said.

DOJ’S ‘OPERATION GHOSTBUSTERS’ TARGETS MASSIVE STUDENT-AID FRAUD SCHEME BUILT ON FAKE ENROLLEES

He also repeatedly lied on federal and state relief applications, claiming he operated multiple nonprofits that employed as many as 10 people when, in reality, he had no employees, according to prosecutors.

In addition, Sellers reportedly claimed to operate a landscaping business and fabricated tax forms for returns he had never filed with the IRS.

GOP LAWMAKER’S FRAUD CRUSADE TAKES DRAMATIC TURN AS SCANDAL ENGULFS HIS OWN CAREER

"Under U.S. Attorney Williams, we have a mandate to aggressively pursue corrupt public officials, no matter what position they hold or what power they wield," Assistant U.S. Attorney Brett A. Janich said in a statement.

Because the payouts were handled electronically across state lines, Sellers now faces four felony counts of wire fraud alongside strict demands to forfeit the illegally obtained funds.

The maximum penalty for wire fraud is up to 20 years in prison.

The FBI investigated the matter, and assistant U.S. attorneys Brett A. Janich and Ryan S. Rummage are prosecuting the case.

item.title: Aidan Hutchinson breaks silence after season-ending injury and announces decision about continuing celebration
item.description: Aidan Hutchinson broke his silence on Instagram after his torn ACL, promising to return stronger and vowing that jump celebrations are now behind him.
item.content:encoded:
Aidan Hutchinson is making two promises following his season-ending right knee injury that came when he celebrated a sack by jumping into the air and landing on a leg that buckled under him.

Hutchinson on Sunday suffered a torn ACL, which requires surgery and has ended his 2026 season.

Well, the Detroit Lions defensive broke his silence about the injury on his Instagram account on Thursday evening.

LIONS' STAR HURT CELEBRATING SACK OF PATRIOTS’ DRAKE MAYE AS BOTH INJURED ON POSSIBLY SEASON-ALTERING PLAY

And the news that comes out of Hutchinson's message is that he is done with celebrations that require him to take flight.

"I honestly can’t believe it," Hutchinson wrote. "I’ve jumped hundreds of times on a football field and never in a million years did I think this would happen to me.

"But even something like this won’t hold me back.

"I can ask why over and over again, but it’ll never make sense. All I can do is surrender to the path. Only God knows why and I trust in Him.

"Very grateful for all of your prayers and well wishes."

There's wisdom and faith here. But perhaps the smartest thing Hutchinson wrote was next.

"Two things I know for sure," he added.

"1. I always come back stronger.

"2. That’s the last time I go airborne 😁👍

"Hold down the fort 'til I’m back, boys."

And there it is. Hutchinson's learned lesson is that the celebration he's done so many times will not be repeated because the chance of an injury repeat will never go away.

Hutchinson is not going to risk another seemingly preventable injury by continuing to do the thing that got him hurt in the first place.

Hutchinson hasn't been alone, by the way.

New York Giants running back Cam Skattebo said Wednesday he is putting his signature backflip touchdown celebration on the back burner.

ZERO BS. JUST DAKICH. TAKE THE DON'T @ ME PODCAST ON THE ROAD. DOWNLOAD NOW!

There have been no NFL coaches who have forced these changes.

Lions coach Dan Campbell, whose team lost its best pass rusher, said this week he wasn't preventing his players from celebrating in whatever fashion they wished.

And Denver Broncos coach Sean Payton said there are a lot of teachable moments from games every week that he puts on tape and shows his team in a meeting.

But that Hutchinson's injury wouldn't be one of those because he's not going to orchestrate celebrations that are acceptable or not.

But there's apparently no need for coaches to police the situation.

The players are doing it for themselves.

So it would be very hypocritical of me to explain that to different players over the course of my career and not take that advice myself."

Parker's unit has struggled mightily this season. They have allowed 28.2 points per game (30th in the NFL) and 393.8 yards per game (last in the NFL), yielding 239.7 passing yards per game (26th in the NFL) and 154.1 yards per game (last in the NFL). They also don't force turnovers, as their 0.8 takeaways a game are 30th in the NFL.

The rest of the NFC East has been ravaged by injuries and underperformance, yet the Cowboys, despite remaining largely healthy, have been unable to take advantage. The New York Giants lead the division at 5-3-1 despite having started three different quarterbacks after Jaxson Dart's injury.

The Philadelphia Eagles have lost seven games in a row, and Jalen Hurts is out for the season because of blood clots. The Washington Commanders lost Jayden Daniels for some time, among other key contributors for the season.

Yet the Cowboys are 4-6 because of their woeful defense. Parker will hope to see the unit improve with Pettine play-calling.

item.title: Al Gore says climate change supporters 'keep quiet' about their beliefs for fear of retaliation
item.description: Former Vice President Al Gore said supporters of climate action "keep quiet" about their support for fear of backlash amid dwindling polling on the issue.
item.content:encoded:
Former Vice President Al Gore suggested on CNN Thursday that people "keep quiet" about their support for action to address climate change for fear of backlash despite the issue's dwindling support ahead of the midterm elections.

"Inside Politics" host Dana Bash spoke to Gore about the 20th anniversary of his climate change documentary, "An Inconvenient Truth." She noted that while climate change was a major factor during the Obama and Biden administrations, the issue was hardly a factor in Democratic campaigns for the 2026 midterm elections.

"What is your message to 2028 candidates and how much they should talk about it?" Bash asked. 

"And I guess, quite frankly, are you worried that Americans and leaders just don't care as much as they did 20 years ago?"

20 YEARS LATER, AL GORE AND HIS DIRECTOR DEFEND THEIR CONTROVERSIAL CLIMATE MOVIE 'AN INCONVENIENT TRUTH'

"Oh, I think they do," Gore responded. "There‘s a political version of what they call the business world 'greenhushing.' It’s different from 'greenwashing.' Greenhushing is when people continue to do the right thing, but they keep quiet about it, lest the evil Eye of Sauron focus on them. And I think that’s going to change in the wake of this election."

Gore made the comments after several polls showed that climate change ranked near or at the bottom of voters' concerns leading up to the November election. Last month, a Gallup poll ranked climate change last among eleven issues leading up to the midterms, with only 29% of voters considering it "extremely important" and 17% considering it "very important."

A Fox News Poll in September found only 1% of voters viewed climate change as the top issue facing the country. 

Still, Gore maintained that the scientists interviewed in his film were "dead on" in their predictions and told CNN that he believes humanity can still respond to the climate crisis.

BILL MAHER CALLS OUT AL GORE FOR COMPARING TRUMP ADMINISTRATION TO NAZIS

"When the underbrush of argumentation is cleared away and the central choice is revealed as a choice between what's right and what's wrong, then because of how we were created, I believe the outcome becomes foreordained. And I think we're very close to that point now," Gore said.

During the interview, Gore also said he's seen "tremendous momentum" in the right direction regarding climate change since 2006, with only a few instances in the wrong direction.

In a comment to Fox News Digital, Democratic strategist and pollster Doug Schoen agreed with Gore that climate change is still a major issue within the party and will continue to be one in 2028.

"Climate change will be a defining issue in the 2028 Democratic primary for president," Schoen said. "And the 20th anniversary of the film 'An Inconvenient Truth' simply underscores the continuing resonance of the climate issue with Democratic activists." 

AL GORE WARNS ABOUT TRUMP'S 'JIHAD' OF CLEAN ENERGY TRANSITION

Longtime Democratic consultant Julian Epstein disagreed, telling Fox News Digital, "If Democrats try to moralize, shame, virtue signal, they will again lose the public on this. If Democrats propose an austerity plan that goes after carbon, raises prices and does little to develop meaningful alternatives, they will also lose the public.

"Polls have consistently shown that 95% of working-class voters are not for the green agenda if it means higher energy prices," he continued. "What we need is an ‘all of the above’ strategy on energy that keeps prices down while developing as many alternative sources as possible."

item.title: Legendary Las Vegas buffet to close for renovations after rumors swirled of its demise
item.description: Caesars Palace's Bacchanal Buffet in Las Vegas is closing Jan. 4, 2027, for a major renovation of its dessert area and five specialty kitchens. It's expected to reopen in the summer.
item.content:encoded:
Visitors planning a trip to Las Vegas in the near future will miss out on one of the Strip's best-known all-you-can-eat destinations, at least temporarily.

Caesars Palace announced Nov. 18 that its Bacchanal Buffet will temporarily close Monday, Jan. 4, 2027, for a major renovation, according to a news release shared with Fox News Digital.

The closure is expected to last until summer 2027, the hotel said.

BARGAIN BUFFET REFUSES TO DIE WHILE LUXURY DINING TAKES OVER VEGAS

Diners hoping to visit before construction starts have until Sunday, Jan. 3, to dine at the venue.

The upcoming project marks the second restoration for the 25,000-square-foot dining hall since it opened in September 2012, the resort said.

While a 2021 remodel updated several sections, the 2027 renovation will focus on the dessert area and five specialty kitchens serving Italian, Mediterranean, Asian grill and barbecue, sushi and sashimi and regional Asian dishes, the press release said.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

Caesars Palace said the updates will bring new menu options and dining experiences to the Strip venue.

"We’re doubling down on Bacchanal Buffet with this renovation," Terrence O’Donnell, senior vice president and general manager of Caesars Palace, said in the release.

"This next chapter brings fresh flavors and new experiences to the buffet, giving guests even more to look forward to when we welcome them back next summer."

The redesign will incorporate wood counters and shelving, brushed-metal finishes and illuminated onyx panels at the dessert station, the company said. 

News of the months-long shutdown quickly drew mixed reactions among frequent Las Vegas visitors.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE STORIES

"Bacchanal is the first name out of everyone's mouth when someone asks about a Vegas buffet, so a renovation closure is going to surprise a lot of people booking winter trips," one Reddit user wrote.

"I think this is horrible news," another user wrote.

Others wondered why a partial remodel would take six months or so. 

Some even questioned if the buffet would ever reopen.

"I have that fear myself. Six months seems like too long of a time for some minor renovations," another person replied.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Some Vegas fans pointed out, however, that extended construction timelines are standard on the Strip.

"Lengthy renovations are nothing new in Vegas. The question is how much of an improvement it will be," the commenter wrote.

As Fox News Digital reported in the summer, many of the famous buffets of Las Vegas fell victim in recent years to the COVID-19 pandemic, its social-distancing requirements and the trend of wealthier visitors seeking higher-end restaurants.

There were over a dozen traditional Vegas buffets on the Strip in 2020, The Wall Street Journal reported. 

Now, there are just a handful.  

Unlike many Strip resorts, budget casinos rely heavily on repeat local customers and value-conscious gamblers, making inexpensive buffets an effective way to drive casino traffic.

Fox News Digital reached out to Caesars Palace for additional information.

Theresa Mull contributed reporting.

item.title: Cowboys great Michael Irvin outlines franchise's timeline to retain 'America’s Team' status
item.description: Michael Irvin says Jerry Jones' Dallas Cowboys have about 10 years to win a Super Bowl before losing the "America's Team" title to another NFC team.
item.content:encoded:
More than three decades have passed since the Dallas Cowboys last advanced to a Super Bowl. In the years since, the franchise has experienced limited postseason success and has not returned to the NFC Championship Game.

Even so, the Cowboys remain one of the NFL’s most popular teams, frequently appearing in nationally televised windows and routinely drawing prime time interest. Their history, including five Super Bowl titles, which rank second among NFL teams, has helped the franchise retain its widely recognized "America’s Team" moniker.

However, Cowboys Ring of Honor member Michael Irvin says the popular nickname should be retired unless Dallas starts winning.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

Irvin was a key part of the Cowboys’ three Super Bowl-winning teams in the 1990s, a run that built on the "America's Team" status. The retired wide receiver is giving his former team a decade-long runway to prove it should keep the label.

COWBOYS LEGEND DIGS DEEP INTO THE TEAM'S MISSING 'FIBER' THAT'S RESULTED IN SUPER BOWL DROUGHT

"A whole generation goes by and never experiences the glory of a championship story from the Dallas Cowboys," Irvin told CNBC on Thursday. "A generation is considered 40 years in the bible. So the Cowboys got about 10 years [to win a Super Bowl and keep the 'America’s Team' title]."

Irvin wore the famed "star" on the side of his helmet for his entire NFL career and was inducted into the Pro Football Hall of Fame in 2007. He finished his career with more than 11,000 regular season receiving yards.

The Cowboys have missed the postseason in each of the past two seasons and could face another early offseason this year. Dallas is competing in an uneven NFC East, with the Philadelphia Eagles dealing with notable injuries and the Washington Commanders struggling.

COWBOYS STAR QUINNEN WILLIAMS REPEATS SIX WORD ANSWER 12 TIMES IN PRESSER AFTER MAJOR COACHING CHANGE

After the Cowboys' defense faltered again in a 46-40 loss to the San Francisco 49ers last Sunday, defensive coordinator Christian Parker was relieved of his play-calling duties. The Cowboys enter Sunday’s game against the 1-8 Tennessee Titans at 4-6, needing a win to keep their playoff hopes alive.

Parker, 34, spent the previous two seasons as the Eagles passing game coordinator & defensive backs coach.

In the the 10 games he's handled defensive playcalling for Dallas, the team ranks 32 in the NFL in total yards allowed and rushing yards given up. The 49ers put up 584 yards against Dallas in Week 10, the most the Cowboys’ defense has allowed in a home game in franchise history.

item.title: Hasan Piker complains the far left has less leverage with Democratic Party because the Dems won too many seats
item.description: Hasan Piker lamented Democrats' vast midterm margin weakened the far left's leverage, saying a smaller win could have allowed socialists to pressure the party.
item.content:encoded:
Far-left streamer Hasan Piker lamented that Democrats were so successful in the midterms they aren’t as dependent on their far-left flank.

The Democrats won a resounding victory in the midterms, which surprised not only the Republican Party, but the far left. Just a month before the midterms, Piker had talked about using the far left to pressure candidate James Talarico to push progressive policy, saying, "We are the force that allowed him to win this seat of power, and if he wants to maintain it, he’s got to play ball."

On Wednesday night, however, Piker played a different tune, noting that the Democratic Party was so successful it is no longer as dependent on support from its most left-wing members.

HASAN PIKER DECLARES 'WOKE IS BACK,' FANTASIZES ABOUT PUTTING DONALD TRUMP IN PRISON

"I think that there was a way that we could possibly get out of this fight with clear concessions on our agenda. We didn't. Part of that was because nobody expected the margin to be so vast," he said. 

"If the margin was 10, then we could have made an impact. If the Democratic Party's margin of victory was 10 and not like f---ing 40, OK, then yeah, we could have had a big caucus, a socialist caucus, a fighter caucus, whatever you want to call it, that could potentially bully the party to be more responsive to the needs of the masses."

Piker also hit back at some critical comments from his fans.

"’This is you at your worst,'" he read aloud one comment before responding. "Why? Because I have to explain to you as an adult who is a political pundit how, you know, how change never really happens in Washington, D.C.? 

"It hurts your feelings to hear someone explain to you why these things happen while simultaneously telling you how much I oppose it? Does it hurt your feelings to hear how this goes?" he asked. "It's just reality.

"I'm going to continue to explain how the sausage gets made, even if that hurts your f---ing feelings, because you're too dumb to understand."

Republican consultant Mary Marslender reacted to Piker's commentary.

"Hasan Piker is furious that Democrats won too many seats because it weakened the (Democratic Socialists of America's) ability to hold the Democratic Party hostage. Piker’s complaint reveals that the far left prefers narrow majorities so it can force its destructive socialist experiments on our country and European-style street chaos," she told Fox News Digital.

FAR-LEFT STREAMER HASAN PIKER GLOATS AFTER DEM BLOWOUT, PROMISES ‘JAIL’ FOR CONSERVATIVE ENEMIES

Democratic strategist and co-host of "The Huddle" podcast Dan Turrentine told Fox News Digital, "There is the world as Hasan Piker wished it would be, and the real world. Socialists are utterly irrelevant in the next Congress. They are not the majority of America, nor are they the majority of the Democratic Party. 

"In fact, in the next Congress, socialists will be a tiny 2.7% of the House Democratic caucus and there will be only one in the Senate, Bernie Sanders."

item.title: Baltimore DC Anthony Weaver addresses Marlon Humphrey 1-game banishment over city crime remarks
item.description: Anthony Weaver backed Marlon Humphrey's benching, saying freedom of speech doesn't mean freedom of consequence after the Ravens star's podcast remarks.
item.content:encoded:
Baltimore Ravens defensive coordinator Anthony Weaver backed the franchise Thursday after head coach Jesse Minter sent veteran cornerback Marlon Humphrey home and benched him for Sunday's game against Carolina.

Humphrey is a healthy scratch for claiming on his podcast that Baltimore is "best at making criminals." Even after Humphrey apologized Wednesday, Baltimore Mayor Brandon Scott dismissed the remarks as "not enough" before Minter stepped in.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

The controversy has also highlighted a glaring double standard in Baltimore: wide receiver Rashod Bateman continues to play despite facing offseason family violence charges, while franchise icon Ray Lewis is honored outside the stadium with a statue.

RAVENS' RASHOD BATEMAN FACES DOMESTIC CHARGES FOR ALLEGED ATTACK ON CAR CARRYING EX-GIRLFRIEND AND THEIR BABY

Stepping to the podium Thursday, Weaver backed Humphrey's benching.

"This is a learning moment," Weaver said. "In this day and age, I think it's important for these guys to understand that, yes, you have freedom of speech. You can say what it is you want to say, on your phone, on your platform, whatever that is. But that doesn't give you freedom of consequence."

RAVENS PLAYERS RIDE WITH PRESIDENT TRUMP IN MOTORCADE, GET SHOUTOUT DURING SPEECH AT BALTIMORE SHIPYARD EVENT

"I think that's where we're at," Weaver added. "So, we're living in that, regardless of intent. He said the things that he said, which obviously is negative toward where we live and where we love."

Even while endorsing the benching, Weaver distinguished between Humphrey's character and his poor judgment.

MARLON HUMPHREY SAYS MEETING PRESIDENT TRUMP INSPIRED HIM TO VOTE IN THE NEXT ELECTION

"I think as a dad, as a coach, as a Christian, it's important to say that I can love the man, have respect for him, and disagree with what he said in this particular moment," Weaver said.

Running a podcast is easier when you are actually playing well, and Humphrey hasn't been.

"I think it's safe to say that, defensively, we haven't lived up to our standard," Weaver admitted. "So, as it pertains to him individually, I think a lot of his errors have been a product of technique and fundamentals."

"That's weird to say for a guy that's been at his stature for such a long time, but it's one of those things where you're constantly sharpening and making sure your tires are aligned as a player."

"It's very easy to get comfortable and start to let those things go by the wayside a little bit," Weaver said. "When that happens, you give up plays like that. Particularly as you age, you're just not able to rely on your pure athleticism, maybe as you once did."
